We know that if& $A \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) \text{ and } B \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)~lies on the same side to line~$L = 0$, then~{L}_{A \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\r$rright)}{L}_{B\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)} > 0$.

Given, the points~$A \left(1, 2\right) & B \l$left(sin\theta,cos\theta\right)~lies on the same side of the line~$x + y - 1 = 0$.

$∴ \left($1 + 2 - 1\$right)\l$left(sin\theta +cos\theta -$1\right) > 0$

$⇒ $sin\theta +cos\theta$> 1$

$⇒ $sin\theta \times \dfrac{1}{2} +cos\theta \times \dfrac{1}{2}$> 1 $\times \dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ $sin\theta .cos\dfrac{π}{4} +cos\theta .sin\dfrac{π}{4}$> $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ $sin \left(\theta + $\dfrac{π}{4}\right)> \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{π}{4}< \left(\theta + \dfrac{π}{4}\right) < \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

$⇒ 0 < \theta < \dfrac{π}{2}$

$⇒ \theta \in \left($0, \dfrac{π}{2}\right)$

$

questions.q: Suppose that the points  \left(h, k\right), \left(1, 2\right)$ and  \left(-3, 4\right)$ lie on the line ${L}_{1} .$ If a line ${L}_{2}$ passing through the points  \left(h, k\right)$ and  \left($4, 3\right)$ is perpendicular to ${L}_{1},$ then $\dfrac{k}{h}$equals:$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Slope of line ${L}_{1}$ is $\dfrac{4 - 2}{- 3 - 1} = \dfrac{2}{- 4} = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$
Hence slope of ${L}_{2}$ is $2 .$
From line ${L}_{1}, \dfrac{k - 2}{h - 1} = \dfrac{- 1}{2}$
$⇒ h + 2k = 5$ …..(1)
From line ${L}_{2}, \dfrac{k - 3}{h - 4} = 2$
$⇒ k = 2h - 5$ ..…(2)
From (1) and (2) $h = 3$ and $k = 1$
$⇒ \dfrac{k}{h} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.q: Let  \left(5, \dfrac{a}{4}\right)$, be the circumcenter of a triangle with vertices $A ( a, - 2 ) , B ( a, 6 )$ and $C  \left(\dfrac{a}{4}, -2\right)$. questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: $A \left(a, - 2\right), B \left($a, 6\$right)\$ttext{and}C\$left(\dfrac{a}{4}, -2\right)$

$⇒ AB^{2} = \left($a - a\right)2 + \left($6 + 2\right)2$

$⇒ AB^{2} = 64 . . . \left($i\right)$

$⇒ BC^{2} = \left($a - \dfrac{a}{4}\right)2 + \left(6 + 2\right)2$

$⇒ BC^{2} = $\dfrac{9a^{2}}{16} +$64 . . . \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ AC^{2} = \left(a - $\dfrac{a}{4}\right)$2 + \left(-$2 + 2\right)2$

$⇒ AC^{2} = $\dfrac{9a^{2}}{16} . . . \left($iii\right)$

Using \left(i\right), \left(ii\right)\text{and}\left($iii\right)$,

$⇒ AC^{2} + AB^{2} = BC^{2}$

So, $△ ABC$ is right angled at $A$.

So, circumcentre will be mid-point of $BC$.

$⇒ S ≡ \left(\dfrac{a + \dfrac{a}{4}}{2}, \dfrac{6 - 2}{2}\right)$

$⇒ S ≡ \left(\dfrac{5a}{8},2\right) = \left($5, $\dfrac{a}{4}\right)

$⇒ a = 8$

$⇒ BC = $\sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 64}{16} + 64}

$⇒ BC = $\sqrt{100} =$10$

$⇒ AB = 8$

$⇒ AC = $\sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 64}{16}}

$⇒ AC = 6$

Now, circumradius is given by,

$R = $\dfrac{BC}{2} =$5 ⇒ $\alpha =$5$

Now, area of triangle will be \beta = \dfrac{1}{2} \times$6 $\times$8 = 24$ and perimeter will be \gamma =$6 + 8 + 10 = 24$

$⇒ $\alpha =$5, $\beta =$24, $\gamma =$24$

$⇒ $\alpha + \beta + \gamma =$53$

$

questions.q: If the two lines $x +  \left(a - 1\right)y = 1$ and $2x + a^{2}y = 1, \left(a \in \mathbb{R} - \left\{0,1\right\}\right) are perpendicular, then the distance of their point of intersection from the origin is$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
If two lines& ${a}_{1}x + {b}_{1}y = {c}_{1}$~and~${a}_{2}x + {b}_{2}y = {c}_{2}$~are perpendicular, then~${a}_{1}{a}_{2} + {b}_{1}{b}_{2} = 0 .$

Since, given lines~$x + \left(a - 1\right)y = 1$~and~$2x + a^{2}y = 1$~are perpendicular, hence, we get

$1 ⋅ 2 + \left(a - 1\right) ⋅ a^{2} = 0$

$⇒ a^{3} - a^{2} + 2 = 0$

$⇒ \left(a + 1\right) ⋅ \left(a^{2} - 2a + 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ a = - 1$~or~$a^{2} - 2a + 2 = 0$

But, the discriminant of the quadratic equation is~\left(- 2\right)2 - 4 \times 1 \times 2 = 4 - 8 = - 4,$~hence, no real roots exist.

Thus, the only possible value of~$a$~is~$- 1 .$

And, hence the lines are $x - 2y = 1$ and $2x + y = 1 .$

Point of intersection of these two lines is \left(\dfrac{3}{5}, - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)$

We know that, the distance of a point~ \left(x, y\right)$ from origin is~$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$
Hence,~distance of the point~ \left(\dfrac{3}{5}, - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)$ from origin $= \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{25} + \dfrac{1}{25}}= \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}} .

$

questions.solution:
In& $△ ABC, AB = AC$

Solving~$2x + y = 4 \text{ and } x + 3y = 7$, we get~

$B ≡ \left(1, 2\right)$

Let~$C ≡ \left(h, k\right)$~and as it lies on~$2x + y = 4$

so~$2h + k = 4$

Now, $AB^{2} = AC^{2}$

$26 = ( h - 6{)}^{2} + \left(k - 1\right)2⇒ 26 = \left(h - 6\right)2 + \left(3 - 2h\right)2$

$⇒ 26 = 5h^{2} - 24h + 45$~$⇒ \left(h - 1\right)\left(5h - 19\right) = 0$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{19}{5}$~ ~ (as~$h = 1$rejected)

so~$k = - \dfrac{18}{5}$

Hence, centroid~$= \left(\dfrac{6 + 1 + \dfrac{19}{5}}{3}, \dfrac{1 + 2 - \dfrac{18}{5}}{3}\right)≡ \left(\dfrac{18}{5}, - \dfrac{1}{5}\right)

i.e.~15\left(\alpha + \beta\right) =$15 $\times \dfrac{17}{5} =$51$

Let, $B ≡ \left(p, 0\right)$

$⇒ AB = p + 1, p > 1$

Now, finding point $C$ using parametric form we get,

\dfrac{x + 1}{cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}} = \dfrac{y - 0}{sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}} =$p + 1$

$⇒ C ≡ \left(\dfrac{- p}{2} - \dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{3}{2}\left(p + 1\right)\right)$

$⇒ BC^{2} = \left(\dfrac{- 3}{2}\left(p + 1\right)\right)2 + \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\left(p + 1\right)\right)2$

$⇒ BC = \sqrt{3} \left(p + 1\right) = $4\sqrt{3}

$⇒ p = 3$

So, $C ≡ \left(-3, $2\sqrt{3}\right)

Now, equation of line $BC$ is given by,

$y = $\dfrac{- 1}{3} \left(x - 3\right)$

Solving with line $y = x + 3$.

$⇒ x + 3 = $\dfrac{3 - x}{3}

$⇒ $x\sqrt{3} +3\sqrt{3} =$3 - x$

$⇒ x \left(\sqrt{3} +1\right) = 3 \left($1 - \sqrt{3}\right)$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{3 \left($1 - \sqrt{3}\right)}{1 + \sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{- 3}{2} \left(4 - $2\sqrt{3}\right)

$⇒ \alpha = -3\left(2 - $\sqrt{3}\right)\text{and}\beta = -$3 + $3\sqrt{3}

$⇒ $\dfrac{\beta4}{\alpha2} = \dfrac{81\left(\sqrt{3} - 1\right)4}{9\left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)2}

$⇒ $\dfrac{\beta4}{\alpha2} = \dfrac{9\left(4 - 2\sqrt{3}\right)2}{\left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)2}

$⇒ $\dfrac{\beta4}{\alpha2} =$36$

$

questions.q: A man starts walking from the point $P ( - 3, 4 ) ,$~touches the $x$-axis at $R,$~and then turns to reach at the point $Q ( 0, 2 ) ,$~The man is walking at a constant speed. If the man reaches the point $Q$ in the minimum time, then $50  \left((PR{)}^{2} + ( RQ{)}^{2}\right) is equal to ______ .$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
For minimum time, value of $PR + RQ$~must be minimum

so~$R$~lies on $PQ^{'}$(where~$Q^{'}$is image of~$Q$~w.r.t~$x$-axis)

From the diagram we can easily say~$Q^{'} ( 0, - 2 )$

As we know that~ \left(y - {y}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}}{{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}}\left(x - {x}_{1}\right)$

Equation of~$PQ^{'} \left(y + 2\right) = $\dfrac{4 + 2}{- 3 - 0}\left($x - 0\right)$

$⇒$ Equation of$PQ^{'}$ is $2x + y + 2 = 0$

For the coordinate of point $R$ put~$y = 0$

$⇒ R \left(-1, 0\right)$

$⇒ 50 \left((PR{)}^{2} + ( RQ{)}^{2}\right)$

Distance formula~$= $\sqrt{{( {x}_{2} - {x}_{1} )}^{2} + {( {y}_{2} - {y}_{1} )}^{2}}

$⇒ PR = $\sqrt{{( - 3 + 1 )}^{2} + {( 4 - 0 )}^{2}}$& RQ = $\sqrt{{( 0 + 1 )}^{2} + {2}^{2}}

$= 50 ( 20 + 5 ) = 1250$

$

questions.q: Consider the triangles with vertices $A \left(2, 1\right), B  \left($0, 0\right)$~and $C  \left($t, 4\right), t = \left[$0, 4\right]$. If the maximum and the minimum perimeters of such triangles are obtained at $t = $\alpha and $t = \beta$~respectively, then $6\alpha +$+21\beta$is equal to ___________.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

The triangles with vertices $A \left(2, 1\right), B \left($0, 0\right)$~and $C \left($t, 4\right), t = \left[$0, 4\right]$,

And~the maximum and the minimum perimeters of such triangles are obtained at $t = $\alpha and $t = $\beta~respectively,

Now to minimise $CA + CB$,~in below diagram take image of $B$ in~$y = 4$,

We get,~$B^{'} = \left(0, 8\right)$

~

Now finding, equation of~$AB^{'}$~we get,

$y - 8 = \dfrac{- 7}{2} \left(x - 0\right)$

Now, putting~$y = 4$~in above equation we get,

$- 4 = \dfrac{- 7}{2} \left(x\right)$

$⇒ x = $\dfrac{8}{7}$⇒ \beta = $\dfrac{8}{7}

Now, maximum~perimeter~will be possible if~$\alpha =0$~or~$4$

Now taking~$\alpha =0$~we get,

$AB = $\sqrt{5},$BC = 4 \text{ and } AC = $\sqrt{13}

Now when $\alpha =4$~we get,

$AB = $\sqrt{5},$BC = $4\sqrt{2}$ \text{ and } AC = $\sqrt{13}

Now on comparing the perimeter we get, maximum perimeter at~$\alpha =4$

Hence,~$6\alpha +21\beta =48$

$

questions.q: Consider a triangle $\mathrm{ABC}$ having the vertices $\mathrm{A}(1,2), \mathrm{B}(\alpha, \beta)$ and $\mathrm{C}(\gamma, \delta)$ and angles $\angle A B C=\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $\angle B A C=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$. If the points $\mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{C}$ lie on the line $y=x+4$, then $\alpha^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to ________
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Equation of line passes through point $\mathrm{A}(1,2)$ which makes angle $\frac{\pi}{6}$ from $y=x+4$ is $\begin{aligned} & y-2=\frac{1 \pm \tan \frac{\pi}{6}}{1 \mp \tan \frac{\pi}{6}}(x-1) \\ & y-2=\frac{\sqrt{3} \pm 1}{\sqrt{3} \mp 1}(x-1) \\ &
\oplus\oplus
y-2=(2+\sqrt{3})(x-1)y-2=(2-\sqrt{3})(x-1)
\\ & \text { solve with } \mathrm{y}=\mathrm{x}+4 \quad \text { solve with } \mathrm{y}=\mathrm{x}+4 \\ & x+2=(2+\sqrt{3}) x-2-\sqrt{3} \quad x+2=(2-\sqrt{3}) x-2+\sqrt{3} \\ & x=\frac{4+\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}} \quad x=\frac{4-\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}} \\ & \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \alpha^2+\gamma^2=\left(\frac{4+\sqrt{3}}{1+\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\frac{4-\sqrt{3}}{1-\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 \\ & \alpha^2+\gamma^2=14\end{aligned}$
